fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test and avoid excess nitrogen. In autumn, a 5% urea spray on fallen leaves speeds their breakdown and reduces overwintering spores.
treatment: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves; prune to open the canopy; plant scab-resistant varieties where possible.
eco_friendly_treatment: Sulfur or lime-sulfur protectant sprays during wet spring periods.
chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as captan or mancozeb from green tip; myclobutanil from green tip to petal fall.
notes: Caused by Venturia inaequalis. Infection needs wet leaves in spring, so protectant sprays work best when applied before rain.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; keep potassium adequate and avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: Prune out dead wood and cankers; remove mummified fruit from the tree and the ground; keep the orchard floor clean.
eco_friendly_treatment: Copper-based spray at dormancy combined with strict sanitation.
chemical_treatment: Captan or thiophanate-methyl from bloom through summer.
notes: Caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa, which survives in cankers and mummified fruit.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test. No specific nutrient controls rust.
treatment: Remove nearby juniper / eastern red cedar hosts where practical; plant rust-resistant apple varieties.
eco_friendly_treatment: Sulfur sprays during the spring infection period.
chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil or mancozeb from pink bud through early summer.
notes: Caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae, which needs both apple and juniper to complete its life cycle.

fertilizer: Apply a balanced fertilizer in early spring based on a soil test.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring, pruning and orchard sanitation.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Use an acid-forming nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate; blueberries need acidic soil (about pH 4.5-5.5).
treatment: No treatment needed. Mulch with pine bark or sawdust and keep soil evenly moist.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces soft growth that is more susceptible; otherwise fertilize according to a soil test.
treatment: Prune to improve airflow; avoid overhead irrigation; remove root suckers.
eco_friendly_treatment: Sulfur, potassium bicarbonate or neem oil sprays at the first sign of disease.
chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil or trifloxystrobin at the first sign of disease.
notes: Caused by Podosphaera clandestina. Unlike most leaf diseases, powdery mildew does not need wet leaves to infect.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring and pruning.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test with balanced nitrogen and adequate potassium; avoid nutrient stress.
treatment: Rotate away from corn for 1-2 years; bury or break down infected residue; plant resistant hybrids.
eco_friendly_treatment: No effective organic spray; rely on crop rotation, residue management and resistant hybrids.
chemical_treatment: Strobilurin (e.g. azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin) or triazole (e.g. propiconazole) fungicide around tasseling to silking when disease pressure is high.
notes: Caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis; survives in corn residue and is favoured by warm, humid weather.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test. No specific nutrient controls rust.
treatment: Plant resistant hybrids; early planting can help the crop escape peak rust periods.
eco_friendly_treatment: No effective organic spray; resistant hybrids are the main control.
chemical_treatment: Azoxystrobin, propiconazole or mancozeb, generally only warranted when infection is severe before tasseling.
notes: Caused by Puccinia sorghi. Spores are wind-blown over long distances, so crop rotation has little effect.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test with balanced nitrogen and potassium; avoid nutrient stress.
treatment: Rotate crops; bury or manage infected residue; plant resistant hybrids.
eco_friendly_treatment: No effective organic spray; rely on rotation and residue management.
chemical_treatment: Propiconazole, azoxystrobin or pyraclostrobin around tasseling when the disease is present.
notes: Caused by Exserohilum turcicum; survives in corn residue.

fertilizer: Split the nitrogen application (part at sowing, part around the knee-high stage); apply phosphorus and potassium according to a soil test.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine scouting.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes dense, humid canopies.
treatment: Remove mummified berries and infected canes; prune and position shoots for airflow.
eco_friendly_treatment: Copper sprays (limited efficacy) combined with strict sanitation.
chemical_treatment: Mancozeb, myclobutanil or captan from bud break to veraison.
notes: Caused by Guignardia bidwellii; overwinters in mummified berries.

fertilizer: Balanced nutrition; avoid water and nutrient stress.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected wood and dead vines; prune in dry weather; disinfect pruning tools.
chemical_treatment: No curative fungicide. Protect pruning wounds with a registered wound-protectant product.
notes: A trunk disease complex (Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp.). Leaf symptoms come from wood infection, so leaf sprays do not help.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test with adequate potassium.
treatment: Remove fallen infected leaves; improve canopy airflow.
notes: Caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis clavispora).

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer; adjust potassium and magnesium using soil or petiole tests.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine canopy management and monitoring.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Maintain good nutrition, including micronutrients (zinc, manganese, iron) where deficient. This may help tree vigour but does not cure the disease.
treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected trees to limit spread; plant certified disease-free nursery stock; monitor for Asian citrus psyllid.
eco_friendly_treatment: Horticultural oil or neem oil to suppress psyllids.
chemical_treatment: No cure. Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector with approved insecticides (e.g. imidacloprid).
notes: Caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). It is a regulated disease in many regions; check whether suspected cases must be reported.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: Plant resistant varieties; use windbreaks; avoid overhead irrigation.
eco_friendly_treatment: Fixed copper at low rates (copper can injure peach leaves, so follow label rates).
chemical_treatment: Copper sprays at leaf fall and dormancy; oxytetracycline during the season where registered.
notes: Caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni.

fertilizer: Apply a balanced fertilizer in early spring based on a soil test.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring and pruning.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test with adequate calcium and potassium; avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: Remove badly infected plants; use certified disease-free seed and transplants; rotate 2-3 years away from pepper and tomato; avoid overhead irrigation.
notes: Caused by Xanthomonas spp. Copper-resistant strains are common in some areas, which reduces the effect of copper sprays.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; adequate calcium and even watering help prevent blossom-end rot.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Keep nitrogen and potassium adequate; nutrient-stressed plants are more susceptible.
treatment: Rotate crops; remove plant debris; avoid overhead irrigation.
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb; azoxystrobin under heavy disease pressure.
notes: Caused by Alternaria solani.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; avoid excess nitrogen and keep potassium adequate.
treatment: Destroy infected plants immediately; use certified seed tubers; hill soil over tubers; destroy cull piles and volunteer plants.
chemical_treatment: Protectant mancozeb or chlorothalonil; on an outbreak, products such as metalaxyl-M + mancozeb or cymoxanil.
notes: Caused by Phytophthora infestans, which can spread rapidly through a field in cool, wet weather.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test with split nitrogen application.
treatment: No treatment needed. Keep scouting, especially in cool, wet weather when late blight risk is high.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer in early spring; well-rotted compost.
treatment: No treatment needed. Remove old fruiting canes after harvest.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Phosphorus and potassium according to a soil test. Nitrogen is normally supplied by Rhizobium root nodules; inoculate seed in fields new to soybean.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine scouting.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen; otherwise fertilize according to a soil test.
treatment: Plant resistant varieties; space plants for airflow; remove heavily infected leaves.
eco_friendly_treatment: Sulfur, potassium bicarbonate or neem oil sprays at the first sign of disease (sulfur can injure plants in hot weather).
chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil or trifloxystrobin at the first sign of disease.
notes: Caused by Podosphaera xanthii.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: Remove infected leaves; renovate beds after harvest; use drip irrigation; plant resistant varieties.
eco_friendly_treatment: Sanitation (removing infected leaves and old foliage) is the main organic control.
notes: Caused by Diplocarpon earlianum.

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer; light nitrogen after renovation.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring.
notes: No disease detected.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test with adequate calcium and potassium; avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: Remove badly infected plants; use disease-free seed and transplants; rotate crops; avoid overhead irrigation.
notes: Caused by Xanthomonas spp. Copper-resistant strains are common in some areas, which reduces the effect of copper sprays.

fertilizer: Keep nitrogen and potassium balanced; avoid nutrient stress.
treatment: Remove lower infected leaves; rotate crops; mulch to prevent soil splash; stake plants.
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb; azoxystrobin under heavy disease pressure.
notes: Caused by Alternaria solani.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; avoid excess nitrogen.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants; avoid overhead irrigation; destroy volunteer plants.
chemical_treatment: Protectant mancozeb or chlorothalonil; on an outbreak, products such as cymoxanil or metalaxyl-M combinations.
notes: Caused by Phytophthora infestans, which can spread rapidly in cool, wet weather.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test.
treatment: Reduce humidity and improve ventilation, especially in greenhouses; remove infected leaves; use resistant varieties.
notes: Caused by Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum); favoured by high humidity.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test.
treatment: Remove lower infected leaves; rotate crops; mulch; avoid wetting the foliage.
notes: Caused by Septoria lycopersici.

fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen, which can favour mite populations.
treatment: Keep plants well watered (mites thrive in hot, dry conditions); remove heavily infested leaves.
eco_friendly_treatment: Insecticidal soap or neem oil; release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).
chemical_treatment: A miticide such as abamectin or spiromesifen; rotate modes of action to slow resistance.
notes: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), a pest rather than a disease. Broad-spectrum insecticides can make outbreaks worse by killing natural predators.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test.
treatment: Improve airflow; remove crop debris; rotate crops.
eco_friendly_treatment: Copper-based fungicide may give partial control; sanitation is the main non-chemical measure.
notes: Caused by Corynespora cassiicola.

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer to maintain plant vigour; fertilizer does not cure the virus.
treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants; use resistant varieties; protect nurseries with insect-proof netting.
eco_friendly_treatment: Yellow sticky traps, reflective mulch and neem oil against whiteflies.
chemical_treatment: No cure. Control the whitefly vector with insecticides such as imidacloprid or pyriproxyfen.
notes: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, spread by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci.

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer to maintain plant vigour; fertilizer does not cure the virus.
treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants; disinfect tools and wash hands; use resistant varieties and certified seed.
eco_friendly_treatment: Sanitation: remove infected plants and disinfect tools and hands.
notes: Tomato mosaic virus spreads by contact (hands, tools) and through infected seed.

fertilizer: Fertilize according to a soil test; adequate calcium and even watering help prevent blossom-end rot.
treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring.
notes: No disease detected.
